newsitem.title: UK: L-Bank taps popular lira to broaden investor base.
newsitem.headline: L-Bank taps popular lira to broaden investor base.

text.p: Germany's L-Bank on Wednesday further widened its investor base ahead of EMU with a well-received euro-tributary lira Eurobond, J.P. Morgan said as joint lead manager of the transaction.
"We are sold out...most of the paper has gone into Italy," a new issues trader at J.P. Morgan said, adding there was little investor overlap with buyers of prior L-Bank euro-linked deals.

Today's issue, for 500 billion lire and also jointly led by Caboto, can be redenominated into euros post-EMU after which it will be fungible with L-Bank bonds in francs and marks launched earlier this year.

L-Bank vice-chairman Christian Brand told bankers at a conference here recently that providing euro product at the earliest possible stage was important because it did not have a branch network and wanted to establish itself with investors.
Brand said it would be important for borrowers to have a liquid yield curve in euros ready for January 1999, but not at any cost.
"There was no downside for us (in the franc and mark bonds). The deals worked on their own. We did not (have to) leave any money on the table to make sure they worked".
Like those previous financings, the lira deal stood on its own, syndicate managers said.
"There has been a tremendous increase in institutional (investor) activity in the lira in the past six months," the J.P. Morgan trader said.
"Investors want more liquidity and borrowers have begun to provide it," she added. "It (lira market) is much more important than it used to be...and not just another Aussie dollar market."

Lira bonds have performed well over the past 12 months on a pre-EMU rate convergence play. The 10-year BTP/Bund spread is now just below 110 basis points from around 135 b.p. a month ago and 285 b.p. this time last year.
Despite that improvement, Italian interest rates were still high enough to require a slight fudge on the L-Bank pricing.
Euro-tributary, or parallel, bonds have feeder issues, with the same maturity date, in more than one EU currency. They have clauses allowing for their fungibility after redenomination.
Most carry the same coupon, one lower than would be seen in Italy. Launching a lira bond with the same low coupon, at a deep discount, would lead to a taxable capital gain for Italians.

So today's L-Bank lira deal, like an EIB funding last week, was given a higher initial coupon, in both cases 9.00 percent, which will step down to the level of the other feeder deals on the coupon date in 1999.
Euro offerings accounted for five percent of the international bond market in the first six months of the year, according to Capital DATA Bondware.
First-half figures showed 55 deals worth $20 billion were launched. The bonds were launched in eight European Union currencies including the Ecu.

The third stage of European economic and monetary union, including the introduction of the European Union's planned single currency, the euro, is prescribed by EU law to take place no later than January 1, 1999.
From that date, all national currencies within the euro area will cease to exist legally and will instead be expressions of the euro.
